summary: As the canonical RFC format changes from plain text to XML, several publication formats will be rendered from it. This informational document defines the HTML format that will be rendered for an RFC or Internet-Draft.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 7992 defines a Hypertext Markup Language (HTML) format for published RFCs and Internet-Drafts. It specifies the page structure and how Extensible Markup Language (XML) source appears in HTML.

subtitle: The HTML structure and rendering rules for RFCs and Internet-Drafts.

tldr.problem: As the canonical RFC format moves from plain ASCII text to XML, the RFC Editor needs a defined HTML publication format.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7992 specifies a strict HTML subset, UTF-8 output, document structure, stable anchors and mappings from XML elements to HTML.
tldr.outcome: The HTML output is non-canonical and the RFC expected details to change as publication tools developed; the supplied metadata says RFC 9920 updates it.

today: RFC 7992 is an Informational document published in December 2016 and has been updated by RFC 9920. The RFC itself expected details to change as the publication tools developed.

sections.title: Why RFCs Have an HTML Format
sections.content:
The RFC Series is changing from canonical plain-text ASCII to XML that can be rendered in several publication formats. RFC 7992 defines the HTML format used for RFCs and Internet-Drafts.

The format is a strict subset of HTML, and a CSS file embedded in each HTML document controls its visual layout. The RFC warns that details may change as the publication tools are developed.
sections.plainLanguage: RFCs can be published as web pages generated from structured source files. This memo defines the page structure and leaves visual style to embedded rules.

sections.title: Requirements for the HTML Format
sections.content:
The HTML must work in supported browsers and display adequately in at least one text-based browser. It must be self-contained, without external files for images, CSS or JavaScript, so it can be moved over email, FTP or rsync without breaking.

The format supports stable, linkable anchors for headings, paragraphs and other elements. JavaScript has limited use and cannot overwrite or change text already rendered in the HTML; accessibility requirements cover screen readers, color perception and small screens.
sections.plainLanguage: An RFC HTML file must carry its own required resources and work in text-based browsers. Its key information must remain accessible on small screens and to people using assistive tools.

sections.title: HTML Version and Syntax
sections.content:
The starting HTML version is HTML5. The output must be valid HTML encoded as UTF-8, and attribute values use double quotes unless HTML rules forbid quoting.

Logical lines end with a line feed; tabs, form feeds and carriage returns are forbidden. These formatting rules are intended to make text-comparison tools easier to use, not to change how the page looks.
sections.plainLanguage: The HTML must use UTF-8 and valid HTML5 syntax. Consistent line endings and quoting make different versions easier for tools to compare.

sections.title: Anchors, Pilcrows and Page Structure
sections.content:
An XML anchor becomes an HTML id. Paragraphs, artwork and source-code segments outside figures and tables receive a linked pilcrow mark (U+00B6), which is normally hidden until the element is pointed at.

The document begins with HTML5 front matter, metadata and embedded CSS. It can include a local style sheet named rfc-local.css; the body and back matter are rendered according to element-specific rules, with author information and an optional index at the end.
sections.plainLanguage: Stable IDs let readers link directly to parts of a document. A pilcrow is a link mark added to many paragraphs so they can be referenced individually.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
RFC HTML files may be copied and opened outside a normal web-browser environment, such as from a local mirror. The RFC therefore limits features such as JavaScript and external resources.

The format's security rules are tied to keeping the document self-contained and limiting what its HTML can do. The memo describes those constraints as part of the format requirements.
sections.plainLanguage: RFC HTML can be copied and opened locally, so it must limit features that could create security problems. The RFC restricts JavaScript and external resources.
